newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia extends debate on first broadcast bill.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia extends debate on first broadcast bill.

text.p: Parliament has extended debate on Indonesia's first broadcast bill to take into account new technologies and media such as the Internet, the chairman of the parliamentary broadcast committee said on Friday.
Abu Hasan Sazili also rejected recent suggestions in the media that the committee was under pressure from private broadcasters to prevent state-owned television from carrying advertising.
"It's not true that privately owned television stations have lobbied us strongly not to allow (state-owned) Televisi Republik Indonesia (TVRI) to carry advertising," he told Reuters.
The government submitted a draft broadcasting bill to parliament in March. Parliament had been expected to approve it by mid-October.
Sazili said, however, that debate had been extended to allow further discussion of such telecommunications developments as cable television, the Internet and other multi-media applications.
Sazili said he expected state-owned television to begin carrying selected advertisements, but added that the parliamentary committee was still discussing the matter.
The country's five privately owned television stations are expected to face strong competition for advertising revenue when TVRI starts carrying advertisements.
TVRI is the country's oldest television station with the largest network and coverage.

Three of the privately-owned stations, Rajawali Citra Televisi (RCTI), Televisi Pendidikan Indonesia (TPI) and Surya Citra Televisi (SCTV), are controlled by relatives of President Suharto. Well-connected businessmen control the two remaining stations.
Indonesia's advertising market has grown rapidly and is likely to continue to boom in coming years, a report by London-based Zenith Media said last week.

It said about $668 million was spent on television advertising in Indonesia in 1995, a 29 percent increase from 1994. It forecast the figure would rise to $770 million this year and $1.5 billion by 2001 at 1995 prices.
